newsitem.title: USA: US investors expect EMU on time despite skepticism.
newsitem.headline: US investors expect EMU on time despite skepticism.

text.p: Growing doubt about the plan to form a single European currency in 1999 swept through U.S. financial markets on Friday, but most investors still clung to the view that the euro will be launched on time, experts said.
The German Finance Ministry and Bundesbank denied a rumor that Germany was about to make a statement saying the start of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) would be put off.
"I sense that some market participants are questioning whether there will be a delay," said an analyst at a top Wall Street firm. "But that certainly isn't the consensus."
"The consensus within the market remains that delay would be a major blow to the entire EMU process, and therefore, it's very unlikely," the analyst said.

The analyst noted that evidence that EMU is expected to begin on time can be found by looking at the German and French money market curves, which are trading virtually on top of each other on a forward basis.
"As a barometer of the markets' expectation that EMU will likely take place, that suggests to me that the markets are pricing in a fairly high certainty of that event," the analyst said.
Germany and France have led the march towards the single curreny, but lately some investors have begun to question even Germany's ability to qualify for EMU.

German unemployment jumped to 4.66 million in January, the highest since the 1930s. Next week, a flood of German economic figures are due out including February employment data, industrial and production numbers for January and fourth-quarter gross domestic product (GDP).
Experts will scrutinize this data and keep an eye on negotiations on Germany's new tax plan for any clues about progress towards EMU, which is scheduled for January 1, 1999.

The consensus view is still that EMU starts on time, but there is growing concern about whether Germany has such budget problems that it may be unable to meet the Maastricht criteria, said Chris Widness, an international economist at Chase Securities Inc.
The Maastricht Treaty limits public deficits to 3.0 percent of GDP and debt to 60 percent of GDP for those countries hoping to qualify for the single currency.
Some U.S. investors' concerns about EMU centered on the possibility that the countries will not adhere to a strict interpretation of the Maastricht criteria.

"As far as: Will they adhere hard and fast to the Maastricht criteria? Will they adhere fast to the time(table)? I think it's all subject to a good deal of watering down if the leadership issue is seriously put in doubt as far as Mr. Kohl's standing is concerned...," said John Krey, chief investment strategist at Barclays Global Asset Management.

Soaring unemployment in Germany has increased political pressure on German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, Europe's longest serving head of government. The German newspaper Berliner Morgenpost reported Friday that Kohl is prepared to stand in the 1998 general elections for what would be his fourth term.
The German chancellery was not immediately available for comment on the newspaper report, which followed weeks of speculation over whether Kohl will stand in the general elections next year.

As for doubts about adherence to Maastricht guidelines, the analyst said, "That's unfortunately also in the market quite heavily. Most observers of the German, French, Italian and other fiscal balances all expect (the balances) will exceed the 3.0 percent Maastricht criteria this year."
Yet the analyst also said the EMU stability pact would guarantee that those countries starting the euro would need to meet even stricter fiscal targets in subsequent years.
"And hence, the fact that they may miss it by a few tenths of a percent in 1997 isn't particularly troubling," the analyst added.
European heads of state hammered out the stability pact last December in Dublin.
((-- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1668))
